opus-5.5.text:
Well, the short answer is cost, and it compounds in ways that aren't obvious at first. In a latent diffusion model, the denoising network runs many times per image. If you double the spatial resolution of the latent, you quadruple the number of tokens or feature positions. With attention layers, the cost grows roughly quadratically with token count, so memory and compute blow up very quickly. On a data-center GPU that's painful. On a phone, which is where a lot of our work is aimed, it's simply not feasible.

There's also a quality issue people don't always expect. These models are trained at a particular latent resolution, and their sense of global layout is tied to that scale. If you just enlarge the latent at inference time, you often get repeated objects, duplicated faces, broken composition, because the receptive field no longer covers the whole scene the way it did in training. To fix that properly you'd have to retrain or heavily fine-tune at the larger size, and that means more data, more compute, and a bigger model to deploy.

So instead of brute-forcing it, we kept the latent at the size the model handles well and treated higher resolution as a separate problem. We let the diffusion model do what it's good at, which is semantics, composition, coherent structure at a manageable scale. Then we recover the fine detail and the extra pixels with more efficient mechanisms, such as better decoding and upsampling strategies, or refinement that focuses only where detail is needed instead of reprocessing the whole image at full cost.

The broader philosophy is that you shouldn't pay a quadratic price for every pixel when most of the high-frequency information can be reconstructed far more cheaply. Separating the "what goes where" from the "how sharp does it look" gave us a much better trade-off between quality, speed, and memory, which is what really matters if you want these models running on real devices.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says increasing latent resolution causes memory and compute to grow sharply, making larger latents costly.

r002.rationale: It links the higher compute cost of larger latents to speed as a trade-off and says avoiding brute-force scaling improves speed.

r003.rationale: It explains how doubling latent resolution increases token count, but does not state that the baseline scales latent-space size proportionally to target output resolution.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so the obvious thing to do when you want a higher-resolution output is just to make the latent bigger. If you're generating at 512 and you want 1024, you scale the latent grid accordingly and let the diffusion model run on that. The problem is that this is a terrible trade on a mobile device. The cost of the denoising network, especially the attention layers, grows roughly quadratically with the number of latent tokens, so going from 512 to 1024 means something like four times the spatial positions and a much larger blow-up in compute and memory. You're running that network twenty, thirty, fifty times depending on the sampler, so every bit of overhead in a single step gets multiplied. On a phone, where you have a fixed power envelope and thermal limits, that quickly becomes seconds per step, or it simply doesn't fit in memory at all.

The second issue is that the model wasn't trained at that latent size. These models learn a particular statistical distribution over a particular grid, and when you just inflate the grid you tend to get repeated structures, duplicated objects, inconsistent global layout. You can mitigate that with fine-tuning, but then you're paying training cost for every resolution you want to support, and you still haven't solved the compute problem.

So we took the view that the diffusion model should do what it's good at, which is getting the semantics and the composition right at a resolution where it's efficient, and then we handle the resolution separately. We kept the latent at the native size, and the extra resolution comes from a lightweight upsampling stage, essentially a super-resolution network that is far cheaper than even one step of the diffusion model. It runs once, not fifty times, and it's a convolutional model that maps very nicely onto the NPU. You get the high-resolution image, the fine texture, the sharp edges, but you decoupled it from the expensive iterative part of the pipeline.

It's really a systems argument more than a modeling argument. On the device, you're optimizing end-to-end latency and energy, not just quality, and once you look at it that way increasing the latent size is almost never the efficient place to spend your budget.

r001.rationale: It says the larger latent grid causes a major increase in compute and memory, potentially making the model not fit in memory on a phone.

r002.rationale: It describes the increased cost per denoising step and says generation can take seconds per step on a phone.

r003.rationale: It describes scaling the latent grid to match the target resolution, using 512-to-1024 as an example.

astra-6.text: Increasing the latent-space size would make the generation process much more computationally expensive. You have more spatial locations to model, and that increases both memory use and inference time. We wanted higher-resolution images without paying that cost throughout the entire generation process. So the idea was to keep the latent representation compact and let the decoding stage produce the higher-resolution output.

r001.rationale: It says a larger latent space increases memory use.

r002.rationale: It says a larger latent space increases inference time, making generation slower.

r003.rationale: It does not state that the baseline scales latent-space size proportionally to target resolution.

sol-6.1.text: Increasing the latent-space size would make the generation process much more expensive. You have more spatial locations to model, which increases both computation and memory requirements. We wanted to improve the output resolution while keeping that generative process efficient. So the idea was to keep the latent representation compact and let the decoder handle the additional spatial detail.
